In Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE '26), Munich, Germany, October 12-16, 2026. ACM, pp. 4493-4503. doi:10.1145/3832783.3834536
Conference — ASE '26, 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering, Munich (ACM proceedings, pp. 4493-4503)
New Jersey Innovation Institute, Newark, USA (Villani); New Jersey Institute of Technology, Newark, USA (Kellogg)
Proposes an approach; secondary: Evaluates — proposes the command coding methodology and evaluates it in a single-case exploratory case study (all2md library, one senior engineer)
Command coding (authors' own methodology); no version. Related to but distinguished from SDD: 'The most important novelty of command coding is its reliance on cross-model review'

Human-written design artefacts before implementation, serving as a 'constitution': system architecture document (component diagram, data flow, technology stack, interface contracts), pattern library (base classes, configuration patterns, naming conventions), security requirements (threat model, input validation policies), quality standards (coverage targets, documentation, code style). Worklist of atomic work items (identifier, description, dependencies, acceptance criteria, complexity estimate, context files), a human-maintained living document. Cross-model AI review documents. Tests, CI quality gates (linter, type checker, static analysis, security scanners)

Phase 1 Architecture, design, scaffolding and environment setup (human-led) -> Phase 2 Select work items (design decomposed by LLMs into a worklist, human-curated and prioritised) -> Phase 3 Implementation cycles (AI-executed; context packing, then TDD-style loop) -> Phase 4 Code and documentation review cycles (automated gates every commit, cross-model review every 3-5 work items, human review); findings become new work items. In practice daily sprints (morning planning of 3-5 items, AI implementation, afternoon cross-model review, end-of-day integration) and weekly holistic subsystem reviews (Fig. 2, Fig. 3)

Human authors architecture and design artefacts; human reviews LLM-generated worklist in detail and sets priorities; human approval for architecture changes, security implementations, API design; intervention when agents are stuck, tests pass but approach seems wrong, or architectural deviation; human review of security-critical code, API design, architectural alignment and test adequacy (including test logic); weekly holistic reviews
Full workflow (applied over the whole all2md development, 504 commits, 150+ review cycles)

Not classifiable; authors relate command coding to SDD (humans as architects, AI as implementers) but do not classify it. Design documents act as a 'constitution' guiding AI work (closest to spec-first)
Essentially greenfield: a small existing internal utility (~3,300 lines) extended into a comprehensive library ('essentially greenfield - no legacy constraints')

Single project: ~88,000 logical SLOC production (88,352) + ~90,000 test SLOC + ~37,000 lines documentation; 41 parsers, 25+ renderers, 233 test files; 504 commits over 48 calendar days (41 working days). Text also says 'about 45 working days' and 'over 170,000 total lines' (p. 5)
Document conversion library (all2md: 40+ formats to/from Markdown, AST, plugin system, MCP server) for AI/LLM workflows; Python
One senior engineer (the first author); methodology requires senior-level skills (5-10+ years)

Calendar time (48 days) and working days (41, counted as 2.0 person-months); commits per day (12.3); AI API cost (~$550); total actual cost ~$41,500 vs estimated traditional cost $1.2M-$2.4M; estimated traditional effort (COCOMO II 81-164 PM, FPA 40-80 PM, triangulated 60-120 PM); acceleration factor 25-40x. Criterion: production-quality outcomes (static metrics) and acceleration vs estimated traditional effort, with no success level stated; no independent acceptance tests. - Command coding + Claude Code + Claude Sonnet 4 / 4.5 (implementation; Sonnet 4 for docs), with GPT-4.1/5/5.1 and Gemini 2.5 Pro / 3 Pro via direct API for cross-model review: 88k SLOC in 41 working days; coverage 87%, type coverage 100%, 0 lint, 0 security issues, CC grade A (5.04), MI grade A (54.7); cost ~$41,500 (AI API ~$550); 25-40x estimated acceleration. Verdicts: quality and cost: no criterion stated by the authors

No controlled comparison. Single-case exploratory case study; 'baseline' is estimated traditional (non-AI) effort from COCOMO II and FPA (no counterfactual team). Sensitivity check (estimate 50% too high, actual effort 50% higher -> >15x). Held constant: N/A. Acceptance tests: N/A (project's own test suite, 87% coverage). Repetitions: 1. Human intervention: by design (methodology)
Against parametric estimates only: 25-40x acceleration (conservative; >15x under aggressive adjustments); cost reduction 96-98% ($41,500 vs $1.2M-$2.4M). No significance testing

Partly: estimate-based comparison only; authors note no counterfactual exists; COCOMO II calibrated on 1990s-2000s projects with subjective parameters; FPA designed for business applications; methods 'agree within a factor of two'; not repeatable beyond the single case

Single senior engineer (first author, motivation bias); self-reported effort; single-case, favourable conditions (pattern-based, well-documented domain, clear testable requirements, modular, greenfield); may not generalise to legacy projects, other domains, engineers or models; COCOMO/FPA construct validity; coverage is not test quality; static analysis unsound. Contextual quality contagion is a hypothesis needing controlled experiments. Future: replicate in other domains, other engineers/teams, tighter control; which quality gates are most effective
